opening.headline: When learning indicators improve but actual performance does not, learn how to read what the gap means.
body: The learning loss in the tuning task screen is steadily going down. However, when I try using a new input, I don't see the improvement as expected. It is easy to mistake learning indicators for success, so the question becomes what to look at to determine whether you have learned well.

In this class, we'll look at what overfitting is, what it signals when the learning and validation curves widen, and how to counter it with early termination, checkpoints, and data enrichment. Next, we look at examples of the optical illusion that occurs when learning data is mixed in the evaluation set and how to read the two indicators together.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain signs and causes of overfitting
The gap between learning indicators and verification indicators can be distinguished.

screens.title: Learning indicators are good, but actual performance does not increase.
screens.lead: Read what the person in charge had to say about the tuning process. If you look at what's strange, you'll see the question for this class.

paragraphs: The training loss graph in the Tuning Job screen steadily goes down. The person in charge thought that the learning was going well and waited for the task to be completed. However, when I added new inputs to the completed model, I did not see the expected improvement.

If you look at the learning metrics alone, it looks like success. However, learning metrics only tell you how well a model does on training data, not whether it does well on input that it has never seen before. So what should we look at and judge whether we have learned well?
The answer is an indicator measured from data that was not used for training, that is, a validation indicator. This class covers how to read the discrepancies between learning and validation metrics.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: A student who memorizes the answers to a practice problem in its entirety will get a perfect score on that problem, but his or her skills will be revealed when he or she solves a problem he or she has never seen before. The same thing can happen to models.

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Think about it: A time when learning metrics and actual performance were misaligned.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have there ever been discrepancies between learning metrics and actual performance? Did you keep verification data separate at that time?
items.answer: If verification data had not been set aside, there would likely have been no way to detect discrepancies. If you upload validation data when submitting a training job, you can receive both statistics during training.

items.prompt: Did the validation metrics also improve, or did only the learning metrics improve?
items.answer: If both indicators improve together, it means generalization is happening, and if only the learning indicator improves, you may be memorizing it. This distinction is the key to today's lesson.

items.prompt: How diverse was the data in that experience?
items.answer: When the data is small or diverse, the model becomes easier to memorize. The same thing happens if you repeat the same data for too long. Both causes are covered in the screens that follow.

screens.outro: Let’s start by explaining what overfitting is.

screens.title: What is overfitting?
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: overfitting occurs when a model memorizes its training data and performs poorly on new inputs. The ability to perform well on inputs absent from training is called generalization. There are two main causes of overfitting: insufficient or insufficiently diverse data, and repeating the same data for too long during training. A checkpoint provides a safeguard against overfitting. generalization may improve early in training before giving way to memorization, so intermediate model versions are saved separately. In reinforcement fine-tuning, rewarding accidentally correct answers can mean that the learning signal becomes noise, causing a similar problem.

terms.tip: This is a state in which the model memorizes the training data and does not generalize well to new inputs. Training metrics are good, validation metrics are bad.
This is the ability to achieve good performance even with input that was not used for learning. The real goal of tuning is performance on new inputs, not training data.
This is an intermediate model created at the end of each epoch during training. You can select and use the model at the time when verification was best.

terms.term: repeating the same data for too long
terms.tip: This is a case where there are too many epochs. As you continue to scan the training data, the model will memorize the examples.
In reinforced fine tuning, if the model receives a high reward just for guessing, correct inferences are not reinforced and the value depends on luck.

screens.outro: Now let's read in action what the learning and validation curves look like.

screens.title: The learning/verification curve unfolds
screens.lead: Below is an example study log created for illustrative purposes. Select an underlined passage and an explanation of what it means will appear.

visual.alt: This is a line graph showing the learning loss and validation loss for each epoch, and the two lines diverge after the 4th epoch.

marks.note: This is the initial section. The training loss and validation loss are almost the same, which means that the model has not memorized the training data yet.
This is the end of the section where both losses go down together. The training loss starts to get lower than the validation loss, leaving a bit of a gap.
This is the point where verification loss is lowest. The checkpoint of this epoch is the best candidate for generalization.
The training loss continues to go down, but the validation loss goes up. The larger the gap, the weaker the generalization and the more overfitting is in progress.

screens.outro: Now that we've read the signal from the curve, let's see how to respond.

screens.title: Early termination, checkpoints, and data enrichment
screens.lead: Check how to respond to overfitting by switching between the two states, divided into the learning point and the data.

states.label: Respond at the learning point
states.body:
Early termination is a way to stop learning at a point where the validation loss is no longer getting any better. If you have already completed learning, use checkpoints. Training saves the model at the end of each epoch, so you can select and use the model from the epoch that had the best validation.

In the next training, we reduce the number of epochs. When the model feels more monotonous than expected, i.e. the output has less variety, reducing the epoch by 1 or 2 is a guided adjustment. Change the learning rate multiplier or batch size only one at a time to distinguish the effects.

states.label: Correspondence from data
states.body:
Data enrichment is a way to add diverse and balanced examples. If the cause of overfitting is small or indiverse data, it is more fundamental to augment the data rather than change the learning settings. Quality is more important than quantity, so avoid simply repeating the same types of examples.

Enhanced fine tuning is a little different. Evaluation results should start with fluctuations rather than sticking to the lowest and highest. The model must already be successful to some extent in order to have something to reinforce, and the structure must be difficult to guess so that learning is not swayed by chance success.

screens.outro: Now let's practice reading indicators through an example.

screens.title: Case Description: The optical illusion of training data mixed with the evaluation set.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the hypothetical case step by step. Click the following button to see how the illusion was created and how to respond.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: After creating the training data, I copied some of it and created an evaluation set. This was a choice made to save the effort of collecting evaluation sets separately. When the learning was completed and the evaluation was conducted, the evaluation results were very high.

steps.title: cause
steps.body: This means that the model has re-solved the input it has already seen. This measures memorization ability, not generalization ability. Since the evaluation set is a copy of the training data, the model simply returns the answers it memorized.

steps.title: result
steps.body: In actual operation, input that was not included in the training comes in. So operations do not show as much improvement as seen in the evaluation. Because the evaluation results were high, problems were discovered late.

steps.title: response
steps.body: Evaluation data is removed before learning and is never used for learning. Even when modifying or increasing learning data, we manage it so that it does not affect evaluation purposes. By grouping and dividing into original units, you can prevent derivatives of the same original from being mixed on both sides.

steps.title: lesson
steps.body: Just knowing that your evaluation results are high does not give you peace of mind. Evidence that assessment data is separate from learning must first be established. Without this basis, high values ​​may be evidence of memorization.

screens.outro: Here's how to diagnose the situation using a combination of two indicators:

screens.title: Case Commentary: How to Read Two Indicators Together
screens.lead: The instructor interprets four combinations of learning and verification indicators one by one. Click the following button to check the meaning of each combination.

steps.title: both are good
steps.body: If both the learning and validation metrics are good, it is likely that generalization was good. In this case, we also make sure that the validation data is separate from the training before making a conclusion.

steps.title: Only good for learning
steps.body: If only the training metric is good and the validation metric is bad, it is a signal of overfitting. Look at the checkpoints and use the model with the best verification, or check the diversity of the data and train again by reducing the epoch.

steps.title: both are bad
steps.body: If both indicators are bad, the learning itself is not done properly. The data quality, settings, and method itself are questionable. If the loss does not go down and converge, a guided adjustment is to try increasing the learning rate multiplier.

steps.title: Verification is only good
steps.body: In rare cases, only the validation metrics are good. This is a signal to suspect that the segmentation may be contaminated or that the validation data may be too easy. Verify that the validation data resembles the distribution of actual operational inputs.

steps.title: the standard for all judgments
steps.body: The standard for judging any combination is an indicator of data that was not used for learning. So, separating verification data from learning is the starting point for all judgments.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We summarize how to read overfitting signals. Read each paragraph and apply it to your learning records.

paragraphs: Overfitting is a condition in which the model memorizes the training data and becomes weak to new inputs. The learning curve continues to descend, but when the validation curve stops or rises, it is a signal; as the interval increases, generalization becomes weaker.

There are three responses: Early termination to stop at the point where verification indicators do not improve, use of checkpoints to select the model at the best point for verification, and data enrichment to add diverse and balanced examples.

It is the verification indicators that tell the true performance. Therefore, it is necessary to separate evaluation data before learning and make it a habit to read learning and verification indicators together.

Going back to the first question in this class, the reason actual performance does not increase even if the learning metric improves is because the learning metric is a value measured from data the model has already seen. To see performance on new inputs, look at the validation metrics, select the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss as a candidate, and check it in a separate evaluation set. The optimal epoch is not determined solely by the interval between the two curves.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: During training, you can receive both learning and verification statistics. Be sure to specify the verification file as well.

checks.intro: Consider the example of evaluation set contamination. You can choose the most appropriate one because of its high evaluation value.
checks.q: After creating the training data, I copied some of it and used it as an evaluation set, and the evaluation value was very high, but no improvement was seen in actual operation. What is the most appropriate reason?
options: The evaluation set was so difficult that it obscured the model’s capabilities.
The operational input is always the same as the training input, so the evaluation set is incorrect.
The evaluation value was high due to the length bias of the grader.
Since the model recalculates input it has already seen, it measures memorization rather than generalization.
checks.explain: If the input used for training is mixed with the evaluation set, the index is inflated because it means solving a problem that has already been seen. You should set aside the evaluation material before learning and do not use it for learning.

wrong.0: It's not that the evaluation set is difficult; rather, it's because the input has already been seen, so it easily comes out high.
wrong.1: In operations, generalization is important because there is input that was not present in learning.
wrong.2: In this case, the cause is not scoring bias, but data shuffling.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. This is a result of measuring memorization, not generalization, because it is a re-solving of input that has already been seen.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Pay attention to the source of the evaluation set. Rethink what an evaluation set made from a copy of your training data measures.

checks.intro: Read the combination of training and validation metrics. All you have to do is pair combination and interpretation.
checks.q: Match combinations and interpretations of learning and validation metrics
right: I wonder if the split is tainted.
Question the data quality, settings, and method itself.
It is highly likely that generalization was good.
Since it is an overfitting signal, check the checkpoint or data.
checks.explain: The standard for all judgments is an indicator of data that was not used for learning. Depending on the combination, generalization, overfitting, data/method problems, and segmentation contamination are identified.
checks.correctFeedback: All four combinations of interpretations were correctly connected.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some interpretations were off. Consider again which metrics come from data that was not used for training.

glossary.def: It works well on training data and is weak on new input.
This is the ability to perform even with input that was not used for learning.
This is a graph showing the change in training loss and validation loss according to epoch.
This is a method of stopping learning at the point when the verification indicator does not improve.
It is an intermediate model that is saved at the end of each epoch.

misconceptions.myth: If the learning loss is low, it is a good model.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the training loss is low, if the verification loss increases, you are memorizing it. Generalizations can only be said when the verification loss goes down together.

misconceptions.myth: If the value of the evaluation set is high, there is no problem.
misconceptions.fact: If the training data were mixed into the evaluation set, memorization ability would be measured. First ensure that your assessment data is separated.

misconceptions.myth: A model that runs through the entire epoch is always best.
misconceptions.fact: Checkpoints at midpoints may be better. Choose the model at the best time for verification.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Verification metrics tell the true performance.
If the curve spreads out, it is a sign of overfitting.
Respond with checkpoints, early termination, and data enrichment.
Evaluation data is separated before training.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the basis for saying that our validation data is completely separate from our training data?
